newsitem.title: USA: Feelgood Stock Market Index soars on latest economic data.
newsitem.headline: Feelgood Stock Market Index soars on latest economic data.

text.p: The Feelgood Stock Market Index has turned up, with the latest batch of economic numbers showing that the economy is moving along at a nice pace and there is no reason to fear that inflation is raising its ugly head.
For Wall Street, it was nail-biting time this week as investors walked through a minefield of key economic reports that were sure to set the direction for stocks.
By the end of the week, the Fearful Freddies were celebrating the good news that the economy was growing at a non-inflationary pace, allowing interest rates to hold steady -- a dream scenario.

On Friday, investors rushed to buy stocks, lifting the Dow Jones industrial average by a solid 69.91 points to 5,841.85 in late afternoon trading. This eclipsed the record close of 5,778.00 set on May 22.

The economic numbers were indeed market-friendly as the government reported the Producer Price Index edged up 0.3 percent in August and the Consumer Price Index inched up just 0.1 percent, confirming that inflation was still dormant.
Also, retail sales rose a modest 0.2 percent, suggesting that consumers are not spending at a rate that would spur price increases.

In another report, the jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent in August -- the lowest since March 1989 -- and the average hourly earnings of workers crept up to $11.87 from $11.81 in July. The concern was that as the labour market tightens, workers would be able to push for inflationary wage increases.
The experts said the benign inflation background could propel the Dow Jones index to even higher levels.
"The Dow is on target to reach 6,000 points by year-end," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
"The major clouds overhanging the market have dissipated now that there's no inflation and people are not so sure that the Fed will move to raise interest rates."
Investors had become very nervous that the Federal Reserve was just waiting to pounce on the market with an interest rate hike that could stun economic growth and hurt corporate profits.
The speculation was widespread that the central bank would pull the interest-rate trigger at the Sept. 24 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.
But now, many investors are no longer buying that theory.
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January, when it lowered the federal funds rate by one-fourth of a percentage point to its current target rate of 5.25 percent.

Some experts said the market, which is made up of people who are forever trying to read tea leaves and anticipate what will happen in the future, had unreasonable expectations that the Fed would need to boost interest rates.
The downsizing that has swept corporate America in the last three years has boosted workers' productivity at a time when raw material costs are at rock bottom prices, they said.
There were also other clues. For the last several quarters, the chief executives at many of the top companies have been complaining that there has been no pricing flexibility in today's economy.

"The problem is that the government believes in the unjustified theory that growth and job creation could cause inflation and the Fed has been scaring the market by saying that it may start to raise rates," said Richard Salsman, senior economist at the consulting firm, H.C. Wainwright & Co., Economics Inc.
He said the Fed's policy that a low unemployment rate is inflationary has led to the contradiction on Wall Street that, "Good news about the economy is bad news."
Salsman said that nominal wage increases tend to follow, not lead price increases.
"Inflation is a monetary phenomenon," he said. "Wages do not push prices up; rather prices push wages up."
